# Three things

Here's what caught my attention this week:

### [Fox’s Tubi launches Kickstarter fund for creators, debuts “Mixtape” feature](https://thedesk.net/2026/11/fox-tubi-kickstarter-for-creators-mixtapes-for-users/) (article)

This article talks about [Tubi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tubi) partnering with [Kickstarter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kickstarter) to help finance independent creators work.
This strategy aims to lead to the creation of content younger audiences want, while also meeting the targeting needs of advertisers.
There was also some conversation about Tubi's Mixtapes feature.
This allows for users to curate and share collections of movies and television shows with other users.

### [The Death of Traditional Social Listening?](https://www.linkedin.com/pulse/death-traditional-social-listening-andrew-dawson-m-s--vzfze/) (blog)

This post overviews the current state of [social listening](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_media_analytics).
As more and more platforms begin to close public access to online comments, access to the voice of the consumer is straining the utility of social listening as a form of measurement.
However, the post makes it clear that social listening, even during its 'golden era' was only a snapshot.
There's more to how people feel and behave then what is being reflected via  online posts.
This quote from the article sums up this point concisely:

> Traditional social listening isn't dying because people stopped talking.
> It's dying as a theory of completeness.

I also liked the post's framing of the role social listening in terms of the four questions.

### [New NPR strategic plan prioritizes ‘app-first’ digital infrastructure](https://current.org/2026/11/new-npr-strategic-plan-prioritizes-app-first-digital-infrastructure/) (article)

This article is a look into NPR's strategic plan, which partly is focused on rebuilding it's mobile app experience.
The points made about the impact of algorithms, agentic AI, and building upon rented digital land are worth some further consideration.
The vision of 'building a wider funnel' highlighted in the article was also a point that caught my attention.

Check out the links above for the full story in each item, not just my brief summary and analysis.

# What I found interesting this week

This week, I had to revert a repo back to a previous commit hash due to some breaking code.
Indeed, this doesn't happen very often, so I'm not too use to using `git revert`.
While doing this, I was hit with the following error:

```txt
commit <hash> is a merge but no -m option was given.
```

No idea what this meant.
So, I threw it at Gemini to learn more.
This error was due to the hash I was trying to revert back to being a merged commit.
I learned the `-m` option was required to specify how I wanted to handle the changes added by the merge.
If I wanted to undo all the changes, I needed to use `-m 1`.
An `-m 2` flag was available, but this is only useful if you merged main into a feature branch.

Indeed, I'm team rebase all the way.
I would have mitigated these issues if a rebase was performed rather than a merge.
However, choices were made and the git history was already on the remote server, so I had to work with what I had.
Nonetheless, my unclean history resulted in me learning a little more about git.

Yay, me!
